questions.prompt: A Bernoulli(0.3) source is coded under Hamming distortion with $D=0.1$. Compute $R(D)$ in bits. (tolerance 0.002)
questions.explanation: **Numeric answer: 0.412** (tolerance 0.002). Here R(D) = h₂(0.3) − h₂(0.1) = 0.881 − 0.469 = 0.412 bits. For D ≥ 0.3 the rate drops to zero, because always emitting the more likely symbol already meets the distortion budget.
questions.topic: Computational block

questions.prompt: A Gaussian source with variance $\sigma^2=4$ is coded under squared error with $D=1$. Compute $R(D)$ in bits. (tolerance 0.005)
questions.explanation: **Numeric answer: 1** (tolerance 0.005). Here R(D) = ½ log₂(4/1) = 1 bit. Every doubling of the allowed distortion saves exactly half a bit, and the rate diverges as D approaches zero, which is why a continuous source has no finite lossless rate.
questions.topic: Computational block

questions.prompt: In the Gaussian channel $Y_\gamma=\sqrt\gamma X+N$ with $X,N\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, compute $\operatorname{mmse}(\gamma)$ at $\gamma=3$. (tolerance 0.002)
questions.explanation: **Numeric answer: 0.25** (tolerance 0.002). The posterior variance is 1/(1 + γ) = 0.25. The observation has removed three quarters of the prior variance. In nats, the I–MMSE derivative is one half of this value: dI/dγ = ½ mmse(γ) = 0.125.
questions.topic: Computational block

questions.prompt: For the same channel, compute $I(X;Y_\gamma)$ at $\gamma=3$ in nats. (tolerance 0.002)
questions.explanation: **Numeric answer: 0.693** (tolerance 0.002). Here I = ½ ln(1 + 3) = ½ ln 4 = 0.693 nats. Differentiating gives 1/(2(1 + γ)) = 0.125, which is exactly half the MMSE computed above, as the I–MMSE identity requires.
questions.topic: Computational block
